strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: extending RL-based self-play from single-turn/zero-sum settings to multi-turn, multi-agent scenarios including cooperative games (Hanabi), which differentiates the work from the closest prior baselines (SPAG, SPIRAL).

The two proposed techniques (sum-then-normalize turn-level advantage estimation, and per-role advantage normalization) are clearly motivated by concrete failure modes (long-horizon credit assignment, heterogeneous payoff scales) and are ablated individually with sensible outcomes (agent-specific normalization matters most in asymmetric games).

The generalization evaluation is more interesting than typical game-only papers: testing whether game-trained agents improve established multi-agent frameworks (MAD, AutoGen) on downstream math/QA benchmarks is a novel and relevant test of transferability.

Good reproducibility posture: code/models claimed to be released, full hyperparameters, prompts for all six games, evaluation protocols (MCTS strengths, CFR opponent, 1000 games), and hardware details provided in appendices.
The fixed-opponent ablation (Table 3) convincingly demonstrates that self-play, rather than merely RL against a strong opponent, drives generalization.
Qualitative pattern analysis (role-aware strategy, intent recognition) provides a plausible mechanistic account connecting game training to multi-agent system behavior.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the authors themselves acknowledge the turn-level estimator is equivalent to GAE with gamma=1, lambda=1 and an empirical-mean baseline, and agent-specific normalization is essentially a per-role baseline partition. These are reasonable but standard RL engineering choices rather than fundamental contributions.

Statistical rigor of downstream evaluations is weak. AIME24 (30 problems) and AMC23 (40 problems) yield differences of '10%' corresponding to only 3-4 problems, with no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests. Multi-agent system evaluations (MAD/AutoGen) add further stochasticity, making headline claims of +10.0% AIME and +12.5% GPQA fragile.

Ablation results on downstream benchmarks (Tables 8-10) partly contradict the paper's narrative: several ablated variants (fixed-opponent, w/o turn-level, w/o agent-specific normalization) outperform full MARS on downstream tasks (e.g., Table 9: fix-opponent Tic. reaches 94.80 MATH and 53.33 AIME vs. 92.20/43.33 for full MARS; w/o turn-level reaches 60.00 AIME vs. 46.67). The main text only reports game-return ablations and does not confront these inconsistencies, weakening the claim that both components are critical.

Only one external baseline (SPIRAL) is compared; no comparison to other multi-turn/agent RL methods (e.g., RAGEN-style multi-turn GRPO variants) or to simple supervised alternatives, limiting the strength of the empirical case.

Game environments are quite small (Tic-Tac-Toe is trivially solvable; Mini Hanabi is a heavily simplified variant), and 'generalization' is measured on only three mildly harder held-out variants of the same families; the scope of strategic ability claims is narrow (acknowledged two-player limitation).

Reward design includes non-trivial shaping (format rewards, length penalty, reward rescaling) that could confound the source of gains; the contribution of the auxiliary rewards versus the core advantage estimator is not disentangled.

Single-agent results are mixed: several MARS variants degrade GPQA relative to the Qwen3-4B baseline (e.g., 33.84 vs. 39.39), and the generalist is not uniformly best, suggesting the transfer story is more nuanced than presented.
Pattern analysis is qualitative and cherry-picked from two examples; no quantitative measurement of the claimed emergent skills (e.g., theory-of-mind probes) is provided.
Numerous writing/typographical errors ('A naive ,', 'a intuitive', 'ture' in Table 5, missing repository URL in the reproducibility statement) suggest the manuscript was not carefully polished.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: extending RL-based self-play to multi-turn, multi-agent settings, and including cooperative games (Hanabi) alongside adversarial ones is a genuine differentiator from prior work like SPIRAL/SPAG.

The evaluation covers several complementary angles: strategic ability vs. MCTS/Nash opponents, held-out game generalization, integration into established MAS frameworks (MAD, AutoGen), ablations, and qualitative chain-of-thought analysis.

The core method is simple and clearly described; the distinction between sum-then-normalize vs. normalize-then-sum for process rewards is correctly diagnosed, and the GAE(γ=1, λ=1) equivalence is honestly stated.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail (prompts, hyperparameters, evaluation opponents), and ablation tables report full results across many settings.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the two 'contributions' reduce to (1) reward-to-go with an empirical-mean baseline (GAE with γ=λ=1 and V≈E[R], as the authors themselves admit) and (2) per-role advantage normalization. Both are standard, well-understood RL engineering tricks; neither constitutes an algorithmic advance, and no theoretical analysis is provided for either.

Missing critical baseline: the paper never compares against directly applying RLVR (GRPO) on math/reasoning data, which is the obvious alternative hypothesis for why downstream math scores improve. Without this, the central claim that strategic-game self-play produces transferable reasoning gains is not established — the improvements could reflect generic RL fine-tuning effects.

Evaluation is statistically weak: a single model (Qwen3-4B), apparently a single training seed, and no variance or significance testing. Headline claims are based on tiny benchmark subsets — e.g., a '12.5% gain on GPQA-Diamond' or '10% on AIME' corresponds to roughly 2-3 problems; such deltas are well within sampling noise.

Internal inconsistencies undermine the ablation claims: in the appendix full results (e.g., Table 9 MAD setting), ablated variants frequently outperform the full method (e.g., MARS (Kuhn.) w/o turn-level estimator achieves GPQA 50.00 vs. 41.41 for full MARS), yet the main text selectively claims both components are 'critical'. This cherry-picking pattern recurs across Tables 8-10.

Game-playing results are weak in absolute terms: even after training, MARS agents still lose on average to moderate opponents (negative returns vs. Connect Four MCTS-10, Kuhn Nash, Leduc CFR). The headline '28.7% improvement' is a relative improvement on near-zero baselines, overstating practical strategic competence.

Narrative and polish issues: the abstract and reproducibility statement contain dangling sentences ('publicly available a' with a missing URL); there are multiple typos and grammatical errors ('A naive , we can consider', 'speicialist', 'ture' for 'true'); Figure 1 is largely redundant with Figure 3/Table 1.

The qualitative 'pattern analysis' is anecdotal and cherry-picked — two selected <think> traces are presented as evidence of 'Role-Aware Strategy' and 'Intent Recognition' (Theory of Mind) transfer, which is an unreasonably strong interpretive claim.

Only two-player games with tiny state spaces are studied; given the paper's positioning toward 'real-world multi-agent systems', the gap between the training environments (Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker) and the claimed target capability (general multi-agent reasoning) is large and not bridged with evidence.

strengths: Clear problem motivation: extending self-play RL from zero-sum to mixed cooperative/competitive settings for LLMs is a relevant and underexplored direction, and the paper positions itself well against SPIRAL and SPAG.

The experimental program is broad and reasonably complete: three training games, three held-out OOD games, specialist and generalist agents, integration into two established multi-agent systems (MAD, AutoGen), and full results in the appendix.

Ablation studies are targeted and informative: self-play vs. fixed-opponent training (Table 3) convincingly shows overfitting to static opponents, and the advantage-estimation ablations (Tables 4, 6, 7) support both proposed components, with sensible differentiation across symmetric vs. asymmetric games.

The qualitative pattern analysis (role-aware strategy, intent recognition, Table 2) is a nice touch that goes beyond raw benchmark numbers and connects game-trained behaviors to multi-agent system behaviors.
Good reproducibility posture: implementation stack (ROLL, vLLM, OpenSpiel), hyperparameters, prompts, and evaluation protocols are documented in detail, with a public code/model release promised.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the two proposed techniques are quite simple. The 'sum-then-normalize' turn-level advantage is essentially Monte Carlo returns with an empirical-mean baseline (equivalent to GAE with γ=λ=1, as the authors themselves acknowledge), and agent-specific advantage normalization is per-role group normalization already common in GRPO variants. The framing as two 'novel techniques' overstates the contribution.

Statistical rigor is insufficient: benchmark evaluations use small sample sets (AIME24 = 30 problems, so a 10% 'gain' is ~3 questions; AMC = 8 questions implied by granularity), and there are no error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-seed runs anywhere in the paper. Several claimed gains are likely within sampling noise.

Reported results are internally inconsistent with the headline claims. In the single-agent setting several MARS variants underperform the Qwen3-4B baseline (e.g., GPQA drops for Kuhn and Generalist), and in ablation Tables 9-10 the ablated models sometimes substantially outperform the full method (e.g., 'w/o turn-level' reaching 60.00 AIME vs. 43.33 for full MARS in MAD), which undercuts the ablation narrative. The claim of 'consistent performance gains' is stronger than the evidence.

Only a single base model (Qwen3-4B) and a single scale are evaluated; there is no evidence the approach or its stability benefits generalize to other models or sizes. Training is also short (200 steps) on relatively simple games, leaving questions about scalability to harder, longer-horizon games (acknowledged as a limitation but with no supporting evidence).

Percentage improvements on games are computed on returns that can be negative (e.g., Leduc returns like -0.483/-0.487), making '28.7% improvement' figures difficult to interpret; a clearer, standardized metric should be used.

Writing quality issues suggest a rushed submission: incomplete sentence in the abstract ('publicly available a'), typos ('A naive ,', 'speicialist', 'ture' for 'true' in Table 5), and some awkward grammar throughout.

Baseline coverage is thin: only SPIRAL is compared, and both MAD and AutoGen are used with a single configuration each; comparisons against direct multi-agent RL fine-tuning baselines or simpler alternatives (e.g., fine-tuning on self-generated game transcripts) are missing.

The pattern analysis is qualitative and potentially cherry-picked; no systematic measurement (e.g., frequency of the claimed reasoning patterns across traces) is provided to substantiate the theory-of-mind claims.

strengths: Clear motivation and well-defined problem: long-horizon credit assignment and agent-specific advantage estimation in multi-turn, multi-agent RL for LLMs, which are genuinely underexplored relative to single-agent RLVR

Extensive and well-organized evaluation: strategic ability on training and held-out games against MCTS/NE opponents, transfer to two distinct MAS frameworks (MAD competitive, AutoGen cooperative) across seven reasoning benchmarks, plus failure-mode analysis and qualitative reasoning-pattern analysis

Thoughtful ablations: self-play vs. fixed-opponent learning (showing clear overfitting of fixed opponents), sequential removal of the two proposed components, and controlled decoupling experiments comparing against SPIRAL's RAE with the same games and MARSHAL with competitive-only games, which credibly separates algorithmic from environmental contributions
Comparisons with concurrent related work (MT-GRPO) with both theoretical argumentation (variable-length problem, immediate vs. long-term reward) and empirical validation
Good coverage of implementation details, hyperparameters, prompts, and raw unnormalized results; scaling experiment to Qwen3-8B supports robustness of findings
Honest limitations section acknowledging two-player-only scope and future directions
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the 'turn-level advantage estimator' is essentially a Monte Carlo return with a batch-mean baseline (acknowledged as equivalent to GAE with gamma=1, lambda=1), and 'agent-specific advantage normalization' is analogous to SPIRAL's RAE; both are incremental modifications of GRPO rather than a fundamentally new technique

No variance reporting or statistical significance testing: many headline gains rest on very small benchmark test sets (e.g., AIME24 with 30 problems, AMC23), where differences of 3-10 percentage points correspond to only 1-3 problems; single training runs per configuration further weaken confidence in the reported gains

The single-agent setting shows only modest and mixed improvements (some MARSHAL specialists underperform the Qwen3-4B baseline on GPQA), and the claimed transfer story rests primarily on multi-agent settings where the trend, while consistent, is small in absolute terms on average (3.5%)
Evaluation confined to one model family (Qwen3) and small scales (4B/8B), so generalization of the conclusions across model families is unverified

Auxiliary rewards (format bonus, length penalty) and game-reward rescaling introduce potential confounds; the ablations cover the advantage estimator components but not the reward design's contribution to the transfer results

Only two-player, small-state games; the connection between these 'prototype' games and general multi-agent competence is supported by correlational evidence (failure-mode reductions, qualitative traces) rather than controlled causal analysis

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and timely problem: extending RL-based self-play training of LLMs to multi-turn, multi-agent settings, and the combination of cooperative and competitive games (including Hanabi) is a genuine differentiator over SPIRAL, which is restricted to zero-sum games.

The empirical study is unusually thorough for this area: specialist vs. generalist agents, held-out game generalization, fixed-opponent ablation, component-wise ablations of the two algorithmic pieces, a comparison against the concurrent MT-GRPO, scaling to an 8B model (Appendix D), and a decoupling experiment that separates the contribution of the algorithm from the game selection (Appendix E).

The failure-mode analysis (taxonomy of Cemri et al.) and qualitative reasoning-trace analysis provide some mechanistic support for why game-trained agents transfer to MAD/AutoGen, going beyond raw benchmark numbers.
Implementation details, prompts, and full raw results are provided in the appendix, which supports partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The turn-level advantage estimator is explicitly acknowledged to be Monte Carlo returns with a mean baseline, i.e., GAE with gamma=1, lambda=1; the 'sum-then-normalize' inversion of the DeepSeekMath process-supervision recipe is a small tweak. Agent-specific normalization is essentially equivalent to SPIRAL's concurrent RAE (conceded in Related Work), so the headline contribution is largely a delta over very recent concurrent work.

Downstream gains are modest and likely within evaluation noise. Benchmarks such as AIME24 (~30 problems) and AMC23 make differences of 3-10 points correspond to only a few problems; no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere in the paper, despite multi-agent system evaluations being known to be high-variance. The average improvement across all benchmarks is only 3.5%.

Absolute strategic performance remains weak: even after training, the agent still loses heavily to MCTS/CFR opponents on the held-out games (e.g., strongly negative returns on Connect Four and Leduc Hold'em), so the claim of 'strong strategic ability' is overstated relative to the evidence.
The 'Theory of Mind' and 'intent recognition' claims rest on cherry-picked qualitative examples (Table 2); there is no controlled experiment demonstrating these capabilities.

Missing baselines: no comparison against a straightforward GRPO fine-tuning on reasoning data (the natural control for whether gains come from games specifically vs. any RL fine-tuning), and no non-self-play curriculum control beyond the fixed-opponent ablation.

Consistency and polish issues undermine confidence: sampling temperature is 0.6 in Appendix B but 0.5 in Table 13; the base model is referred to as both 'Qwen-4B' and 'Qwen3-4B'; typos in the hyperparameter table ('ture', 'Lambd'); the Mini Hanabi fixed-opponent ablation is simply missing; the reproducibility statement is truncated mid-sentence.

Scope is narrow: only two-player toy games, a single model family, and only the framework-level MASs MAD and AutoGen; the paper's own discussion concedes that scaling to N-player or realistic social sandboxes is unresolved.

Confounded narrative in places: some of the strongest figures (Figure 1) emphasize large gains, but the raw results in the appendix reveal that many single-agent and MAS differences between SPIRAL and MARSHAL are small or inconsistent across benchmarks.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper evaluates strategic ability against strong opponents (MCTS, Nash/CFR policies), held-out game generalization, transfer to two established MAS frameworks (MAD, AutoGen), and scaling to Qwen3-8B, which together provide substantial support for the central claims.

Thorough and targeted ablation studies: the fixed-opponent vs. self-play comparison (Table 3), component ablations of turn-level advantage and agent-specific normalization (Table 4), and the decoupling experiments separating algorithm vs. game environment contributions (Appendix E) are well designed and go beyond what many papers provide.

The paper compares against the most relevant concurrent baselines (SPIRAL's RAE and MT-GRPO) both theoretically and empirically, and honestly positions its contributions relative to them, including the finding that role separation matters only when return distributions differ across players.

The analysis of emergent reasoning patterns and failure modes (Tables 2, Figure 5) adds qualitative insight connecting game-trained skills (role awareness, intent recognition) to observed MAS behavior, strengthening the transfer claim.
Reproducibility is addressed well: complete hyperparameters, prompt templates, evaluation protocols, and a public code/checkpoint release are provided.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the turn-level advantage estimator is essentially Monte-Carlo return normalization with a batch-mean baseline (the paper itself notes it is equivalent to GAE with γ=λ=1), and agent-specific normalization is closely analogous to SPIRAL's concurrent RAE. The core method is a relatively incremental modification of GRPO, and much of the contribution rests on empirical findings rather than new techniques.

Downstream benchmark evaluations suffer from small sample sizes without statistical treatment: AIME24 (~30 problems) and AMC23 (~30 problems) mean headline gains like '10.0% on AIME' correspond to a few problems, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported anywhere. Given the multi-agent evaluation adds variance, several reported gains (e.g., 46.67 vs 43.33 on AIME) may not be reliable.
Only one model family (Qwen3-4B/8B) is tested; generality of the conclusions across model families/sizes is unverified. The scope is also limited to two-player games, which the authors acknowledge.

It is not fully disentangled how much of the downstream MAS gain comes from multi-agent social skills versus generic RL effects (format compliance, conciseness, longer/structured reasoning). The reward shaping (format rewards, length penalty) and general RL benefits could partially explain transfer; the failure-mode analysis helps but does not settle causality.

Minor presentation and consistency issues: hyperparameter table lists sampling temperature 0.5 while the text says 0.6; typos ('ture', 'GPQA-Dimond', 'an intuitive'); inconsistent model naming ('Qwen-4B' vs 'Qwen3-4B'). A broken link in the reproducibility statement ('publicly available a'). These are individually small but collectively suggest insufficient polish.
